questions.question: What does Amazon S3 stand for?

options.text: Simple Server Storage
Simple Storage Service
Scalable Storage System
Secure Storage Service

explanation.correct: S3 stands for Simple Storage Service — AWS's core object storage offering.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are not the correct expansion of the S3 acronym.

questions.question: What type of storage is Amazon S3?

options.text: Block storage
File storage
Object storage
Archive storage

explanation.correct: S3 is object storage — data is stored as objects (data + key + metadata), accessed via HTTP/HTTPS API, not mounted as a drive or file system.
explanation.why: Block storage = EBS; File storage = EFS; Archive is a use case, not a distinct storage type.

questions.question: What is the maximum size of a single S3 object?

options.text: 5 GB
100 GB
1 TB
5 TB

explanation.correct: A single S3 object can be up to 5 TB in size. For objects larger than 5 GB, Multipart Upload is required.
explanation.why: 5 GB is the threshold requiring Multipart Upload, not the maximum size; 100 GB and 1 TB are both below the actual maximum.

questions.question: Which statement about S3 bucket names is correct?

options.text: Bucket names must be unique within your AWS account
Bucket names must be unique within a region
Bucket names must be globally unique across all AWS accounts
Bucket names can be reused after the original bucket is deleted

explanation.correct: S3 bucket names must be globally unique across ALL AWS accounts and ALL regions worldwide. If anyone anywhere on AWS has that bucket name, you cannot use it.
explanation.why: A and B are too narrow — uniqueness is global, not just per-account or per-region. D is incorrect — deleted bucket names have a reclaim delay and historically may be unavailable for some time.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of Availability Zones that S3 Standard replicates data across?

explanation.correct: S3 Standard automatically replicates data across a minimum of 3 Availability Zones within a region, providing 11 nines of durability.
explanation.why: 1 AZ is S3 One Zone storage classes; 2 AZs would not provide the stated 11 nines durability; 5 AZs is above the minimum.

questions.question: What is S3's durability for the Standard storage class?

explanation.correct: S3 Standard provides 99.999999999% durability — eleven nines. This means you can expect to lose at most 1 object per 10,000 years at 10 million objects stored.
explanation.why: 99.9% and 99.99% are availability figures for other services; 99.999% is five nines, not the eleven nines S3 achieves.

questions.question: What is an S3 object key?

options.text: The encryption key used to secure the object
The unique name/path that identifies an object within a bucket
The IAM permission required to read the object
The checksum used to verify object integrity

explanation.correct: An object key is the unique identifier (name/path) for an object within a bucket. For example, '2024/photos/vacation.jpg' is the key. Together, the bucket name + key uniquely identifies any object in S3.
explanation.why: A describes a KMS key; C describes an IAM policy/permission; D describes an ETag/checksum.

questions.question: What is S3's namespace structure for organizing objects?

options.text: Hierarchical directory tree like a file system
Flat namespace — objects have keys, and slashes simulate folders visually
Relational — objects can reference each other like database rows
Block-based — objects are divided into sectors

explanation.correct: S3 uses a flat namespace — there are no actual directories. The '/' characters in object keys are just part of the key string, but the console displays them as folders for user convenience.
explanation.why: A is how EFS/file systems work, not S3; C describes a database; D describes block storage.

questions.question: What is the default access setting for a newly created S3 bucket?

options.text: Public — anyone can access it
Private — only the bucket owner can access it
Shared — accessible to all users in the same AWS account
Protected — read-only for authenticated AWS users

explanation.correct: By default, all S3 buckets and objects are private. Only the AWS account that created the bucket can access it. You must explicitly configure public access, bucket policies, or ACLs to share with others.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are all incorrect default settings — S3 defaults to private with Block Public Access enabled.

questions.question: How does S3 pricing work for the Standard storage class?

options.text: Fixed monthly fee per bucket
Per GB provisioned per month
Per GB actually stored per month plus request fees
Per hour the bucket is active

explanation.correct: S3 charges per GB of data actually stored (no provisioning needed), plus per-request fees (GET, PUT, LIST, etc.), plus data transfer fees for data leaving AWS. There are no fees for creating a bucket or for data transfer into S3.
explanation.why: A and D don't match (no per-bucket or per-hour charges); B is how EBS works.

questions.question: Which S3 storage class should you use for data that is accessed approximately once per month?

options.text: S3 Standard
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 One Zone-IA

explanation.correct: S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access) is designed for data accessed roughly once a month or less. It has lower storage costs than Standard but adds a per-GB retrieval fee. For monthly access, storage savings outweigh retrieval costs.
explanation.why: Standard is too expensive for monthly access; Glacier Deep Archive takes 12-48 hours to retrieve (fine for once/year, not once/month); One Zone-IA lacks multi-AZ redundancy.

questions.question: When is Multipart Upload required in S3?

options.text: For objects larger than 100 MB
For objects larger than 1 GB
For objects larger than 5 GB
For objects larger than 5 TB

explanation.correct: Multipart Upload is required for objects larger than 5 GB. AWS recommends using it for objects over 100 MB for better performance, but it is only mandatory above 5 GB.
explanation.why: 100 MB is AWS's recommendation threshold, not the requirement; 1 GB is not a threshold; 5 TB is the maximum object size.

questions.question: An S3 bucket was created in ap-south-1 (Mumbai). You switch the AWS console to us-east-1 (N. Virginia). What happens to the bucket in the S3 dashboard?

options.text: The bucket disappears — it only shows in ap-south-1 console
The bucket still appears — S3 has a global dashboard showing all buckets
A replica of the bucket automatically appears in us-east-1
The bucket shows as read-only from other regions

explanation.correct: S3 is a global service with a single dashboard. All buckets from all regions appear regardless of which region is selected in the console. This is unlike EC2, where switching regions changes which instances you see.
explanation.why: A is how EC2 works, not S3; C would require Cross-Region Replication to be configured; D is not how S3 works.

questions.question: A company stores 100TB of data in S3 Standard. Analysis shows 80% of objects haven't been accessed in over 60 days, and 15% haven't been accessed in over a year. What is the most cost-effective multi-class strategy?

options.text: Move everything to S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Keep all data in S3 Standard for simplicity
Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for all data
Use S3 Lifecycle policies: Standard → Standard-IA at 30 days → Glacier Flexible at 90 days → Glacier Deep Archive at 365 days

explanation.correct: Tiered lifecycle policies match storage cost to access frequency. Objects move down tiers automatically, keeping costs minimal without manual management. The 15% yearly access data ends up in Deep Archive (cheapest), the 65% at 60-365 days in Glacier Flexible, and only the active 20% in Standard or Standard-IA.
explanation.why: A removes all data from fast access; B ignores 80% cost savings opportunity; C works but lifecycle policies give more predictable costs for known access patterns.

questions.question: Which S3 storage class has the lowest cost per GB but the longest retrieval time?

options.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 One Zone-IA

explanation.correct: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest storage class on AWS. Retrieval takes 12-48 hours. It is designed for data that must be kept for years or decades but is rarely if ever accessed — compliance archives, raw legal records.
explanation.why: Glacier Instant has millisecond retrieval (higher cost); Flexible is 1-12 hours (middle cost); One Zone-IA is for infrequent access but has sub-second retrieval.

questions.question: What does S3 Versioning do when you delete an object?

options.text: Permanently deletes the object and all its previous versions
Moves the object to the Glacier storage class
Creates a delete marker — the object is hidden but not deleted; previous versions are preserved
Archives the object with a 30-day grace period before permanent deletion

explanation.correct: When versioning is enabled and you delete an object without specifying a version ID, S3 creates a delete marker. The object appears deleted but all previous versions are preserved. To permanently delete, you must delete each version explicitly.
explanation.why: A is what happens without versioning; B and D are not versioning behaviors.

questions.question: What is S3 Intelligent-Tiering and when would you use it?

options.text: A storage class that compresses objects automatically
A storage class that automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage patterns — no retrieval fees
A machine learning service that predicts which objects to delete
A caching layer that stores frequently accessed objects in memory

explanation.correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns and automatically moves objects to lower-cost tiers when not accessed. Unlike Standard-IA, there are no retrieval fees for accessing objects regardless of their current tier. Best for data with unpredictable or changing access patterns.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are not what Intelligent-Tiering does.

questions.question: A developer uploads a file named 'reports/2024/q4-results.pdf' to an S3 bucket. Is there a real directory called 'reports' or '2024' created?

options.text: Yes — S3 creates real directories for each / separator in the key
No — the entire string 'reports/2024/q4-results.pdf' is just the object key; the console shows it as folders for visual convenience
Yes — the directories are created as empty objects
No — slashes are not allowed in S3 object keys

explanation.correct: S3 has a flat namespace. 'reports/2024/q4-results.pdf' is simply the complete key (name) of the object. The S3 console displays it under visual 'folders' as a convenience, but there is no actual directory structure. A 'folder' in S3 is just a 0-byte object with a key ending in '/'.
explanation.why: A and C are incorrect — no real directories exist; D is incorrect — slashes are allowed and commonly used in keys.

questions.question: Your application in ap-south-1 stores objects in S3. A compliance requirement states data must also exist in us-east-1 with no more than 15 minutes lag. Which S3 feature handles this?

options.text: S3 Multi-Region Access Points
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) with S3 Replication Time Control (RTC)
S3 Lifecycle policy with cross-region copy

explanation.correct: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) automatically replicates objects to a destination bucket in another region. S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) provides a 15-minute SLA guarantee for replication completion — exactly matching the requirement.
explanation.why: Multi-Region Access Points route requests, not replicate data; Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads, not cross-region replication; Lifecycle policies don't replicate in real time.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an S3 bucket policy?

options.text: To set the encryption method for stored objects
To define IAM users in the account
A JSON-based access control policy attached to the bucket that defines who can access it and what actions they can perform
To configure S3 storage class transitions

explanation.correct: A bucket policy is a resource-based IAM policy attached directly to an S3 bucket. It can grant or deny access to specific AWS accounts, IAM principals, or the public. It is written in JSON and evaluated alongside IAM user policies when determining access.
explanation.why: A is a bucket encryption setting; B is done in IAM; D is done with Lifecycle policies.

questions.question: S3 provides 99.999999999% durability. Does this guarantee your data is protected from all failure scenarios?

options.text: Yes — 11 nines means your data is completely safe in all scenarios
No — 11 nines covers hardware failures and AZ outages, but not accidental deletion, ransomware, or region-level disasters
Yes — S3 replicates data globally across all regions automatically
No — 11 nines is only an estimate; actual durability is lower

explanation.correct: The 11-nines durability covers hardware failures, AZ failures, and bit rot — S3's internal redundancy handles these. But it does NOT protect against: accidental deletion (use Versioning + MFA delete), ransomware that overwrites objects (use Versioning + Object Lock), region-level disasters (use Cross-Region Replication), or someone with S3 permissions deleting everything.
explanation.why: A is overconfident — durability ≠ protection from all threats; C is false — S3 does not auto-replicate globally; D is false — 11 nines is a real SLA guarantee.

questions.question: What is S3 Object Lock and when would you use it?

options.text: A feature that encrypts objects so they cannot be read without a key
A WORM (Write Once Read Many) protection that prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a specified period
A feature that locks the S3 bucket to prevent new objects from being uploaded
An access control that limits which IAM roles can modify objects

explanation.correct: S3 Object Lock implements WORM protection — once locked, an object cannot be deleted or overwritten for the defined retention period, even by the root account. Used for regulatory compliance (SEC 17a-4, FINRA, HIPAA) that requires immutable records. Two modes: Governance (some principals can override) and Compliance (no one can override, including root).
explanation.why: A describes encryption; C describes bucket policies; D describes IAM — none are Object Lock.

questions.question: You need to serve S3 static website content to users globally with minimum latency. Which AWS service would you combine with S3?

options.text: Amazon Route 53 alone
Amazon CloudFront (CDN) with S3 as the origin
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon ElastiCache

explanation.correct: Amazon CloudFront is AWS's CDN. When combined with S3, CloudFront caches your static content at edge locations worldwide — users are served from the nearest edge, dramatically reducing latency. S3 is the origin; CloudFront is the global delivery layer.
explanation.why: Route 53 handles DNS routing but doesn't cache content; Global Accelerator optimizes network routing but doesn't cache; ElastiCache is for database query caching.

questions.question: A financial services company must retain all transaction records for 7 years and ensure not even administrators can delete them. What S3 configuration achieves this?

options.text: S3 Versioning with a 7-year lifecycle policy
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period
S3 Glacier Deep Archive with a lifecycle rule expiring after 7 years
IAM policy denying s3:DeleteObject for all users

explanation.correct: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode sets WORM protection where the retention period cannot be reduced or removed by anyone — including the root AWS account. This is the only option that guarantees not even administrators can delete the objects. Combined with Glacier Deep Archive for cost, this is the standard solution for long-term financial record compliance.
explanation.why: A uses versioning but doesn't prevent all deletes; C only prevents lifecycle expiration, not manual deletion; D IAM policy can be modified by an account administrator.

questions.question: What is the difference between S3 Standard-IA and S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval?

options.text: There is no functional difference — they are the same storage class with different names
Standard-IA is multi-AZ; Glacier Instant is single-AZ

Standard-IA has higher storage cost but is designed for monthly access; Glacier Instant has lower storage cost and is designed for quarterly access (once per quarter), with the same millisecond retrieval speed
Standard-IA supports versioning; Glacier Instant does not

explanation.correct: Both provide millisecond retrieval and multi-AZ durability. The key difference is access frequency: Standard-IA is designed for monthly access; Glacier Instant is designed for quarterly access (every 90+ days). Glacier Instant has lower storage cost but higher retrieval and minimum storage duration (90 days vs 30 days for Standard-IA).
explanation.why: A is wrong — they have different pricing and minimum storage durations; B is wrong (both are multi-AZ); D is wrong (both support versioning).

questions.question: What happens when you try to upload a 10 GB file to S3 using a regular (single-part) PUT request?

options.text: The upload succeeds — there is no size limit on PUT requests
The upload fails — the maximum object size is 5 GB
The upload fails — single PUT requests are limited to 5 GB; you must use Multipart Upload for objects > 5 GB
The upload succeeds but the file is automatically split into 2 parts

explanation.correct: A single PUT request to S3 is limited to 5 GB. For objects larger than 5 GB (up to 5 TB), you must use the S3 Multipart Upload API, which uploads the object in parts that are assembled server-side.
explanation.why: A is wrong — 5 GB PUT limit is real; B confuses the PUT limit (5 GB) with the max object size (5 TB); D is not automatic behavior.

questions.question: An application generates objects that are accessed 20 times per day for the first week, then rarely accessed after that. Which S3 configuration minimizes cost?

options.text: S3 Standard for all objects
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Standard with a lifecycle rule to transition to Standard-IA after 30 days
S3 Standard with a lifecycle rule to transition to Standard-IA after 7 days

explanation.correct: S3 Standard-IA has a minimum storage duration charge of 30 days — if you move objects there before 30 days, you pay for 30 days regardless. Since objects are active for the first week, moving to Standard-IA after 30 days (just after the 30-day minimum) is optimal — you pay Standard pricing only during active use.
explanation.why: A wastes money after week 1; B works but adds a monitoring fee; D would trigger the 30-day minimum storage charge for objects that lived only 7 days in Standard before transitioning.

questions.question: What is S3 Transfer Acceleration and when would you use it?

options.text: Automatically moves objects to faster storage classes when accessed frequently
Uses AWS CloudFront edge locations to speed up uploads from distant geographic locations to an S3 bucket
Increases download speed by enabling parallel multi-part GET requests
A dedicated network connection between your on-premises network and S3

explanation.correct: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge location, then uses AWS's optimized backbone network to reach the destination S3 bucket. This is significantly faster for uploads from geographically distant locations — a user in Mumbai uploading to a bucket in us-east-1 benefits from edge routing via the nearest CloudFront edge.
explanation.why: A is S3 Intelligent-Tiering behavior; C is Multipart Download / byte-range fetch; D is AWS Direct Connect.

questions.question: You have a public S3 static website. Traffic suddenly spikes 1000x due to a viral event. What happens to the website?

options.text: S3 throttles requests and the website goes down
S3 automatically scales to handle the traffic — no configuration needed
You must pre-provision capacity to handle high traffic
S3 automatically redirects to an EC2 server when overloaded

explanation.correct: Amazon S3 is designed to automatically scale to handle virtually unlimited request rates. There is no capacity provisioning required. S3 can handle thousands of requests per second per prefix. For extreme global traffic, combine with CloudFront to reduce origin requests and add global caching.
explanation.why: A is wrong — S3 auto-scales; C is how EC2 and EBS work, not S3; D is not S3 behavior.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an S3 Access Point?

options.text: A way to access S3 from on-premises without internet
A named network endpoint with its own access policy, allowing different applications to access the same bucket with different permissions
An IAM role that grants EC2 instances access to S3
A VPN tunnel between a VPC and S3

explanation.correct: An S3 Access Point is a named endpoint (hostname) attached to a bucket with its own access policy. Multiple access points on the same bucket can grant different permissions to different applications. For example, one access point for read-only analytics, another for read-write app servers — simplifying permission management at scale.
explanation.why: A is AWS PrivateLink or VPC endpoint for S3; C is an IAM instance profile; D is a VPN connection.
